Bracelets
BRAYS-lets
noun (plural)
From the Old French bracel, a little arm-band, diminutive of the Latin brachium, the arm. Ornaments for the wrist or arm; in Scripture frequently gifts of betrothal, and once a pledge given in shame.

Biblical Definition

Bracelets in Scripture are tokens, and everything depends on who gives them and why. At the well of Nahor, Abraham’s servant, having seen his prayer answered before he had finished praying it, “took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold” (Gen 24:22). They are the earnest of a betrothal, given before Rebekah knows the errand, and Laban’s eye lights on them at once — “when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister’s hands” (Gen 24:30), a detail the narrator includes without comment and which tells us a great deal about Laban. In Judah’s squalid transaction with Tamar the bracelets go the other way: “Thy signet, and thy bracelets, and thy staff that is in thine hand” (Gen 38:18) — a pledge handed over in a moment of appetite and produced months later as evidence, so that a man’s own ornaments convict him. And in Ezekiel they become the emblem of covenant grace: “I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck” (Eze 16:11). Jerusalem is a foundling in a field, unwashed and cast out, and God clothes and jewels her as a bride — which makes the chapter’s later account of her whoredoms all the more terrible, since she took the very jewels He gave and spent them on idols.

Webster 1828 Definition

Ornaments for the wrist or arm; in Scripture tokens of betrothal, pledges of debt, and the emblems of covenant grace bestowed on an unloved bride.

BRACELET, n. An ornament for the wrist; a band or chain worn about the arm.

From the Old French bracel, diminutive of Latin brachium, the arm.

Anciently a piece of defensive armour for the arm.

In Scripture, given as betrothal gifts (Gen 24:22) and as pledges (Gen 38:18).

Figuratively, of the ornaments with which God decks His covenant people (Eze 16:11).

Key Scripture

Gen 24:22 — "And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold;"

Gen 24:47 — "And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter art thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands."

Gen 38:18 — "And he said, What pledge shall I give thee? And she said, Thy signet, and thy bracelets, and thy staff that is in thine hand. And he gave it her, and came in unto her, and she conceived by him."

Eze 16:11 — "I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck."

Modern Corruption

Eze 16 is avoided as too coarse for public reading, which loses the Bible’s most graphic account of grace — a castaway infant washed, clothed, jewelled, and married by God.

expand to see more

The corruption is the sanitising of the covenant story. Ezekiel 16 is rarely read aloud and rarely preached, because it is frank in a way modern congregations find uncomfortable: an abandoned newborn in a field, unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled, left to die; God passing by and saying Live; the child growing, and God spreading His skirt over her and entering into covenant with her; then the clothing, the broidered work, the silk, the jewels, the bracelets, the crown. And then her prostitution, in language that spares nothing. Skip the chapter and you lose the most detailed picture Scripture gives of what grace actually is — not the rewarding of a promising candidate but the rescue of something nobody wanted.

Recover the plain sense: the bracelets are the point of the indictment. God says explicitly that she took His jewels and made images of them, took His broidered garments and covered idols with them, took His oil and His incense and set them before other gods. That is the anatomy of every believer’s besetting sin — the gifts of God turned into instruments against Him. Health, money, intellect, influence, even doctrine and gifts of ministry, are the ornaments He put on our hands, and each may be spent on an idol. And the chapter does not end in the field where it began: God says I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant, that she may remember and be confounded, and never open her mouth any more because of her shame, when He is pacified toward her for all that she hath done.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin brachium, the arm — arm-ornaments; betrothal tokens at a well, a pledge in shame, and the jewels of covenant grace.

expand to see more

Bracelets — Old French bracel, from Latin brachium, the arm.

Anciently also a piece of armour for the forearm.

Gen 24:22: the betrothal earnest given to Rebekah at the well.

Gen 38:18: Judah’s pledge to Tamar, later produced as evidence against him.

Eze 16:11: the ornaments with which God decked the foundling bride.

Usage

"Gen 24:30 notes Laban seeing the gold before he greets the man — character in a detail."

"Judah’s bracelets convict him: a pledge given in appetite, produced in court."

"Eze 16 shows the gifts of God spent upon idols — the anatomy of besetting sin."
